extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, policymakers, tribunal members and scholars working on Canadian and international anti-dumping law and trade remedy procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for initiating, conducting and deciding anti-dumping investigations and provisional measures under Canadian law and the GATT Anti-Dumping Code, including evidentiary, timing, causation and disclosure rules. Focuses on Tribunal practice, relevant statutes/regulations, and GATT/Code requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse dumping duty (proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to levy a duty equal to 100 per cent of the amount by which the price to the Canadian selling organization exceeds the price charged to an equivalent selling organization in the country where the product was manufactured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty collected could be used to subsidize the purchaser to provide the same price treatment as consumers in other markets. To cover multi-location manufacture, the Canadian selling subsidiary would need the right to import from the lowest cost source. The proposal is far-reaching and could apply beyond farm machinery and thus requires careful study before implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of traditional anti-dumping duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional dumping duty is designed to protect manufacturers from competitors who sell in the export market at prices below those prevailing in their home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the protective policy objective against exporters selling below home-market prices; contrasts with reverse-dumping aimed at protecting consumers from higher prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dumping (GATT experts' formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumping: sale by an importer at a price below that corresponding to the price invoiced by the exporter with whom the importer is associated, and below the price in the exporting country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taken from the GATT Experts' Report; provides the baseline factual standard for identifying dumped sales in anti-dumping investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of margin when no domestic sales (Article 2(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2(d) deals with determination of the margin of dumping when 'there are no sales of the like product in the ordinary course of trade in the domestic market of the exporting country or when, because of the particular market situation, such sales do not permit a proper comparison ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 2(d) provides the rule for how to determine normal value or margin where comparison to home-market sales is impossible or unreliable; authorities must apply alternative methods consistent with the Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price comparability and level of trade (Article 2(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2(f) requires comparison of prices at the same level of trade, with allowance for factors affecting price comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons must account for differences in distribution, marketing, or other factors that affect price; adjustments may be required to ensure like-for-like comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation standard — dumping as principal cause (Article 3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 3(a) requires that dumping be 'demonstrably the principal cause' of material injury (i.e., dumping must be the principal, not necessarily sole, cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'thin skull' approach means dumping need not be the only cause; the inquiry is whether dumping is the primary driver of injury. Positive findings are required under Article 3(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat determinations must be fact-based (Article 3(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 3(e) requires that a determination of a threat of material injury shall be based on 'facts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities must ground findings of likely future injury in factual evidence rather than speculation; the standard emphasizes evidentiary support for threat findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of non-confidential information (Article 6(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 6(b) requires the authorities to make available to the parties all non-confidential information used in an anti-dumping investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures procedural fairness and that interested parties can see and respond to the non-confidential evidence relied upon by authorities; confidentiality claims must be managed against this disclosure duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning for provisional measures (Article 10(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 10(c) requires the authorities to inform interested parties of the reasons for their decisions concerning provisional measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities must provide explanations for provisional duties to satisfy Code transparency requirements and enable parties to understand and contest provisional measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit on provisional measures (Article 10(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 10(d) limits the imposition of provisional measures to a ninety day period; the period may be extended to six months 'on decision of the authorities concerned upon request by the exporter and the importer...' but the Canadian Act does not adopt this extension provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ninety-day ceiling constrains provisional measures; Canada's system lacks the extension option, which has created practical difficulties (e.g., in the Steam traps case) when time restraints impede fair process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of respondent information (evidentiary practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information provided by respondents is customarily accepted at face value, unless there is inconsistency with other information from the same or different sources, or other similar reason for scepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where doubts arise, authorities request additional information including original documents; unresolved issues are brought to the panel's attention and addressed through questioning at the hearing. This describes routine evidentiary treatment and verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural flexibility for matters not provided (Rules 33 & 34, SOR/74-581)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 33: 'Where any matter arises during the course of any inquiry or hearing not otherwise provided for by the Act or by the Rules it shall be dealt with in such manner as the Tribunal directs.' Rule 34: 'non compliance with any of these Rules shall not render any proceedings void unless the Tribunal shall so direct, but such proceedings may be set aside either wholly or in part as irregular, or amended, or otherwise dealt with in such manner and upon such terms as the Tribunal shall think fit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants the Tribunal broad discretion to deal with unforeseen procedural matters and to cure or amend irregularities rather than automatically void proceedings for rule breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of import invoices (Customs Act s.172(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 172(3) of the Customs Act: 'In no case shall an invoice be shown or a copy thereof be given to any person other than the importer, or an officer, except upon the order or subpoena of a court of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoices filed at port are protected from disclosure except to designated parties or by court order; this statutory confidentiality affects what documentary evidence can be shared with third parties in anti-dumping proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional duty refund if only likelihood of injury
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Tribunal found that dumping is only likely to cause material injury, the provisional duty is wholly refunded and no final determination of dumping is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between 'likely' and established material injury for treatment of provisional duties. Note: in cases of 'massive importation' duties may be levied for a 90-day period preceding the preliminary determination (s.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines for initiation and completion of investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministerial announcement: 'a decision on whether or not to initiate a formal investigation under the Anti-dumping Act would normally be taken within 30 days from receipt of an adequately documented complaint from Canadian manufacturers, and that investigations would then normally be completed within six months.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets administrative expectations for speed of response; historically waits were often longer before the 1977 administrative guidelines. 'Fast Track' procedures are mentioned as a possible future development.

rubrics_metrics.name: National interest provision (policy exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions' anti-dumping systems contain a 'national interest' provision providing for no anti-dumping duty even although dumping and injury have been shown; such a provision does not exist in Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where present, the national-interest clause has been used in limited contexts (military equipment, international relations) rather than to protect consumers from price effects; its presence is a policy discretion in some systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional industry considerations and impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-dumping actions sometimes consider regional industry impacts (e.g., suspension of duties to protect regional fabricating industry), illustrating difficulty for a large country with dispersed industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions that protect one region's industry can threaten employment in another region; U.S. practice appears to use regional industry concept more often. Policy-makers must weigh national vs regional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of 'the industry' (standing/representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes 'the industry' is a defined issue in proceedings (see discussion and case law such as McCulloch v. Anti-dumping Tribunal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of who represents the domestic industry affects eligibility to complain and the substantive assessment; jurisprudence guides this identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability and judicial interaction on preliminary determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial decisions (e.g., Mitsui v. Anti-dumping Tribunal, Mitsui v. Minister cases) address the extent to which preliminary determinations, conditions precedent and the Deputy Minister's formulations are subject to judicial or tribunal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law shows some disagreement about whether administrative preliminary determinations are fully reviewable; tribunal practice and judicial pronouncements shape the boundaries of review and delegation (e.g., authority to define classes of goods).
